Can you say in the intro to this page how the list is sorted? For example, is it by value, net value after deducting fees, net value after deducting fees and opportunity costs (for example assuming a 2% cash card), or something else?

In the post…

  • “I’ll be taking into account whether a bonus is at it’s highest level ever or not (mostly because I don’t think an offer is truly the best if it regularly goes up to a higher level or I suspect it’ll go to a higher level in the near future).”

I think it would be impossible to have a perfect scorecard/ranking.

Basically I’d say it’s a gut feeling list by the author. What I do is pick a couple to research, and then pounce on one every few-several months. Plenty near the top I skip over all the time because I am not interested due to high annual fees, or don’t think I will get approved. If other people can extract the value w/ travel partners and companion passes, for example, then that’s great.

Not much thought is put into where things are ‘ranked’, I try to do it somewhat but the state specific section in particular isn’t great. Basically if it’s on the list we think it’s worth doing, but outside of that I wouldn’t rely on the order too much. I hope to do a tidy up at some stage but with almost 1,200 new comments today I am not sure when I’ll find the time.

William – Thank you for the enormous effort of assembling this site’s information, including moderating the comments, and keeping the dialogues constructive!

If you ever find the time, you could to order the cards by Net First-year Value, which would equal:
+ Sign up Bonus
– Annual Fee
– Opportunity cost of minimum spend (assume a 2% cashback card).
+ Perks that people are likely to use (this would be subjective, and perhaps should be excluded)

For people wanting to avoid high AFs, you could list the AFs in the table.

Once the table is ordered, it should be comparatively easy to maintain since there will be having to apply gut feel to each new card.
Bit too difficult to assign a value to points and benefits unfortunately.

2 Kroger Pay non-fuel transactions earn 5% cash back on the first $3,000 in purchases each calendar year and 2% on amounts above that. Kroger Pay transactions at Kroger Family of Companies Fuel Centers do not earn rewards. Mobile wallet transactions (excluding Kroger Pay) earn 5% on the first $3,000 in purchases each calendar year and 1% on amounts above that, regardless of where the transaction was made, including Kroger Family of Companies locations. Mobile Wallet transactions at Kroger Family of Companies Fuel Centers do not earn rewards. “Mobile wallet” means Apple Pay®, Samsung Pay, Google Wallet®, and Garmin Pay™. Unlike Google Wallet®, Google Pay® may not qualify as a mobile wallet and earn additional cash back, depending on how the transaction is completed. We cannot control how mobile wallet transactions are designated and reserve the right to determine which purchases qualify for additional cash back. If a Kroger Pay or Mobile Wallet transaction might also qualify as a rewards category transaction, then the card issuer has sole discretion on how to categorize the transaction. “Calendar Year” is defined as the period of time starting with your January statement (which may include transactions made in December) and running through your December statement (which may not include all transactions made in December).
